sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Jesus warns against adopting the posture of condemning judge over others, because the standard one applies to others is the standard God will apply to oneself — a reciprocal principle connected to the forgiveness condition of 6:14-15.
sections.relevance: The reciprocal judgment principle presupposes genuine human agency: a person's choice to judge harshly or mercifully directly determines the standard God applies to that person. God's response is presented as conditioned on human conduct rather than predetermined, implying that human choices genuinely affect one's standing before God.
key_phrases: with the measure you use it will be measured to you
do not judge, so that you may not be judged
the way one treats others determines how one is treated by God

sections.section_title: The Saying About What Is Holy
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that this saying warns against indiscriminate sharing of sacred things with those who will respond with contempt and violence, balancing the preceding prohibition against judging with a call for discernment.

The neutral reading finds that Jesus commands persistent prayer (asking, seeking, knocking) with the promise that the Father — whose goodness far exceeds that of flawed human parents — will respond generously to those who approach him.
sections.relevance: The passage presents God as responsive to genuine human initiative rather than as unilaterally determining who receives. The universal promise 'everyone who asks receives' makes divine generosity available to all who take the initiative to seek, presupposing that humans can and should act and that their actions elicit God's response. While the immediate subject is prayer rather than salvation, the framework of human initiative leading to divine response has implications for the broader question of agency.
key_phrases: ask, and it will be given to you
how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the golden rule serves as the summary conclusion of the entire discourse, identifying active love for others as the essence of what Torah and Prophets demand, closing the frame opened at 5:17.

sections.section_title: The Two Gates and Two Roads
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Jesus presents two paths with ultimate consequences — a wide gate and broad road leading to destruction taken by many, and a narrow gate and hard road leading to life found by few — with the imperative 'Enter through the narrow gate' addressed to hearers as a genuine command.
sections.relevance: The text directly addresses salvation outcomes (life versus destruction) and presents human agency as the differentiating factor. The imperative 'Enter' presupposes the hearers' ability to choose. The verb 'find' implies active seeking by the individual, and the neutral reading explicitly states that 'the few who find the narrow gate are those who have been actively seeking' while 'the many who enter the wide gate are those who take the path of least resistance.' The passage makes hearing the discourse insufficient — human action determines which path one takes. This is part of the author's own argument in the climactic section of the Sermon on the Mount, not an illustration or aside.
key_phrases: the road is hard that leads to life
those who find it are few
the gate is wide and the road is broad that leads to destruction

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Jesus warns against false prophets who disguise themselves as members of the community and provides the 'fruit test' — observable conduct over time — as the reliable method for identifying them.

sections.section_title: The Insufficiency of Profession Without Practice
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Jesus declares verbal confession ('Lord, Lord') and even spectacular spiritual activity (prophesying, exorcising, performing mighty works in his name) insufficient for kingdom entry — the sole criterion is doing the will of the Father.
sections.relevance: The text directly and explicitly addresses who enters the kingdom of heaven, making it a passage about salvation outcomes. The criterion is unambiguously human conduct: 'the one who does the will of my Father.' The neutral reading states this is 'one of the most consequential statements in the entire discourse' and identifies doing the Father's will as 'the sole criterion for entry.' The passage is conventionally cited by both sides — Calvinists point to 'I never knew you' as reflecting predetermined non-election, while those favoring human agency point to 'the one who does the will' as making human obedience the determinant. The neutral reading supports the latter: the rejected are called 'workers of lawlessness' precisely because they did not practice the conduct the discourse defines, not because they were predestined for rejection. Their rejection follows from what they failed to do, not from a prior divine decree.
key_phrases: not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven
but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven
I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the closing parable of the sermon presents two builders who hear the same words but differ solely in whether they act on them — the one who does stands in the eschatological storm, the one who does not collapses utterly.
sections.relevance: The parable directly addresses ultimate consequences (standing versus catastrophic collapse under eschatological testing) and makes human response the sole differentiator. The neutral reading states: 'The sole differentiator is what they do with what they heard.' Both builders have identical access to Jesus's teaching; the difference is entirely in their human response — doing versus not doing. This is the climactic conclusion of the entire Sermon on the Mount, the author's own culminating argument, and it could not present human agency more explicitly: hearing without doing leads to destruction, hearing with doing leads to survival. No divine predetermination of who does and who does not is mentioned or implied.
key_phrases: everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them
everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them
it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock
great was the fall of it

sections.section_title: The Conclusion: Authority Unlike the Scribes
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the author narrates the crowds' astonished reaction to Jesus's teaching, noting that he taught with personal authority rather than by citing precedent like the scribes, and uses this to transition to the demonstrations of authority in chapters 8-9.
